topic: How did Vikings survive -30°C winters with no electricity?

script.text: Ketil hands you a bucket and nods at the door. Water.

You step outside in your hoodie and your sneakers. The air hits you like a wall. You breathe in, and the inside of your nose freezes. That's real. At minus thirty, the moisture in your nose turns to ice in seconds.
At minus thirty, skin that's left bare can freeze in ten to thirty minutes. Add a little wind, and it's under ten. You last about forty seconds before you run back in.
Gudrun sighs, and dresses you like you're five.

First, a long linen shirt against your skin. Then a wool tunic. Wool trousers. Wool wrapped tight around your legs, from ankle to knee. Wool socks made with one needle, a technique called needle binding that the Vikings used. Mittens, the same way.
Wool is the secret. It can soak up about a third of its own weight in water before it even feels wet, and it keeps you warm while it does. Cotton, like your hoodie, does the opposite.

Then a heavy wool cloak, pinned at the shoulder with a brooch. A fur hat. Leather shoes, which Asa stuffs with dry grass, giggling. The grass traps air and soaks up sweat. People in the North did this for hundreds of years.
You step outside again. The cold is still there. But now it's outside the clothes, and you're inside them.

The well is frozen. Ketil smashes the ice with an axe. You fill the bucket. Then you haul firewood. A lot of firewood. A farm like this burns through a mountain of it every winter, and every log was cut by hand.
And you have to do all of it fast. Because in January, this far north, the sun is only up for about five hours.

science.claim: At -30 °C bare skin can freeze in 10 to 30 minutes, under 10 with wind
science.working: Environment Canada wind chill chart: -28 to -39 means frostbite possible in 10-30 min; -40 to -47 in 5-10 min.
science.source: Environment and Climate Change Canada, Wind chill index

science.claim: Wool can absorb about a third of its weight in water before feeling wet
science.working: Wool fibres absorb up to about 30 % of their weight in moisture and release heat while doing so.
science.source: Australian Wool Innovation / The Woolmark Company, wool fibre science

science.claim: Needle binding (naalbinding) used for Viking Age socks and mittens
science.working: Needle-bound textiles are found in Viking Age contexts, e.g. the Coppergate sock from York.

science.claim: About five hours of daylight in January in central Norway
science.working: Trondheim (63.4 N): about 4.5 h on 21 December, about 5-6 h in mid January.
